svg.aria-label: A logarithmic ruler placing twelve latencies on one axis that runs from one nanosecond to one second, ten decades wide. Each latency is a coloured dot on the axis with a stalk rising to a labelled pill, staggered over three rows so that closely spaced events do not collide. Colour groups them: processor work in ink, memory in blue, storage in green, network in gold, and one frame at sixty hertz in orange, drawn with a full-height line because it is the threshold a person can actually perceive. Below the axis a row of six cards restates the same numbers on a human scale, taking one nanosecond to be one second, so an L1 hit is one second, a DRAM access is a minute and a third, a syscall is eight minutes, an NVMe read is fourteen hours, one frame is a hundred and ninety-three days and a cross-continent round trip is four and three-quarter years. Underneath that sits a small strip showing the same twelve points plotted on a linear axis instead, where eleven of them collapse into a single mark at the far left, which is the reason a logarithmic axis is used at all. Closing notes state that the figures are typical orders of magnitude rather than measurements, that a log axis must always be labelled as one because equal spacing means times ten, and that the human-scale column is what makes the difference felt rather than merely read
svg.font-family: Poppins, 'Noto Sans SC', 'Helvetica Neue', Arial, sans-serif
svg.text: ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE · TEN DECADES ON ONE AXIS
every step to the right is ten times longer. that is the only way twelve numbers spanning a factor of 150 million fit in one picture.
the only one a person can perceive
what your eye is waiting for
THE SAME NUMBERS, IF ONE NANOSECOND WERE ONE SECOND
THE SAME TWELVE POINTS ON A LINEAR AXIS · WHY THIS FIGURE IS NOT LINEAR
eleven of the twelve land on this one mark
these are typical orders of magnitude, not measurements — the point is the distance between them, not the digits. measure your own board before quoting any figure.
a log axis has to say so on its face: equal spacing means times ten, and a reader who misses that reads every gap as ten times too small.
the human-scale row is what turns the ruler into an argument. “a hundred thousand times slower” is a phrase; “one second against a hundred and ninety-three days” is a picture.
